extracted.intended_audience: Citizens, legislators, and politically engaged readers considering the U.S. Constitution (People of New York / voters and framers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and normative principles for designing and assessing a senatorial body and its powers under the proposed Constitution (including permanency, selection, treaty-making, secrecy, impeachment jurisdiction, and related safeguards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanency for long-term objects
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional body in the legislative department, having sufficient permanency to provide for such objects as require a continued attention, and a train of measures, may be justly and effectually answerable for the attainment of those objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that annual assemblies and frequently elected numerous bodies cannot reliably manage affairs requiring years to accomplish; a permanent (longer‑tenured) body preserves continuity of information and responsibility. Examples/contrast: projects taking half a dozen years; remedy for defect of short terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smaller body enhances personal responsibility and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sufficiently difficult to preserve a personal responsibility in the members of a numerous body, for such acts of the body as have an immediate, detached, and palpable operation on its constituents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that small councils allow clearer personal responsibility; large legislatures diffuse accountability. Implied design recommendation: make the senatorial body comparatively small to preserve responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as a check on popular passions and temporary errors
rubrics_metrics.description: A temperate and respectable body of citizens [is necessary] as a defense to the people against their own temporary errors and delusions, to check the misguided career, and to suspend the blow meditated by the people against themselves, until reason, justice, and truth can regain their authority over the public mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses historical example (Athens decreeing hemlock one day and statues the next) to justify a deliberative secondary body that can delay or moderate hasty popular measures. Suggests the Senate should be able to 'suspend the blow' until calmer judgment returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation principle must be paired with extensive territory
rubrics_metrics.description: The true distinction between ancient governments and the American governments lies in the total exclusion of the people in their collective capacity from the latter; this advantage must not be separated from the other advantage, of an extensive territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that representative government coupled with a large territory reduces some small‑republic dangers but creates others (longer influence of misrepresentations) — so institutional safeguards like a senate remain necessary. Warns against reasoning from small Greek democracies to the U.S. context without accounting for territory and representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical precedent: long‑lived republics had senates
rubrics_metrics.description: History informs us of no long-lived republic which had not a senate. Sparta, Rome, and Carthage are, in fact, the only states to whom that character can be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses ancients (Sparta, Rome, Carthage) as instructive proofs that some smaller, stabilizing council that blends stability with liberty is necessary. Cautions about literal imitation (lifelong senates repugnant to American genius) but treats the general lesson as supportive of a senatorial institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect election and longer terms to secure ability and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The convention has committed the appointment of senators to the State legislatures and prescribed durations to give them time to become acquainted with national concerns and form a system for management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues indirect election (by state legislatures/select electors rather than direct mass vote) and age/term qualifications (exclusion of men under 35/30) favor men of abilities and integrity, reduce susceptibility to transient popular enthusiasm, and allow accumulation of useful experience. Example: contrast with popular assemblies constantly changing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate competence for treaty-making (selection, experience, and duration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of making treaties should be delegated in such a mode and with such precautions as will afford the highest security that it will be exercised by men the best qualified for the purpose, and in the manner most conducive to the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies treaty-making as requiring talents, exact information, time, and steady pursuit; thus senators chosen by select/legislative bodies, with longer tenure, will be better qualified. Also notes the class of electors and age minimums are prudential safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of secrecy and immediate despatch in negotiations
rubrics_metrics.description: It seldom happens in the negotiation of treaties but that perfect secrecy and immediate despatch are sometimes requisite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that certain intelligence and opportunistic moments (tides in affairs) require secrecy and rapid action. The constitutional arrangement should allow preservation of secrecy (some confidants trusting the President) while providing Senate advice/consent and the President the ability to manage intelligence and convene the Senate when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence between treaties and laws (treaties as binding bargains)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treaties are a bargain; they cannot be altered unilaterally by one party; the proposed Constitution does not extend obligations of treaties beyond their usual reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects the idea that treaties should be merely repealable by domestic legislatures; stresses that foreign nations will not bargain with a country that reserves unilateral repeal. Practical implication: treaties should have force and stability comparable to laws, because alteration requires mutual consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two‑thirds Senate consent balanced and not oppressive
rubrics_metrics.description: The second section gives power to the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur; objections that two thirds will oppress the remaining third are answered by institutional safeguards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses fears that supermajority requirement allows oppression; argues equal state representation and senators' duties reduce likelihood of abuse. Emphasizes public accountability and equal influence of states in the Senate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal state representation defends minority states' interests
rubrics_metrics.description: As all the States are equally represented in the Senate, they will all have an equal degree of influence in that body... In proportion as the United States assume a national form, the good of the whole will be more an object of attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that equal representation in the Senate ensures smaller or less populous states are not oppressed in national negotiations (e.g., treaties), provided states appoint proper persons and insist on attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal responsibility, honor, and impeachment as checks on corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Every consideration that can influence the human mind, such as honor, oaths, reputations, conscience, the love of country, and family affections and attachments, afford security for their fidelity; and so far as the fear of punishment and disgrace can operate, that motive to good behavior is amply afforded by the article on the subject of impeachments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts that personal virtues and institutional impeachment provide safeguards against corruption; points out practical improbability of President and two‑thirds of Senate conspiring corruptly. Notes fraudulent treaties would be null by law of nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as the proper tribunal for impeachment trials
rubrics_metrics.description: A well‑constituted court for the trial of impeachments is difficult to obtain in a government wholly elective; the convention thought the Senate the most fit depositary of this important trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues impeachment jurisdiction should be lodged in a body that is dignified, independent, numerous, and able to preserve impartiality between the accused individual and the people's representatives. Compares British House of Lords model and state examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment tribunal must be numerous and independent (not the Supreme Court)
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of a numerous court for the trial of impeachments is dictated by the nature of the proceeding; the Supreme Court would be an improper substitute because of deficiencies in authority and number, and because the same persons should not decide both the political sentence and subsequent criminal punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains dangers if the same judges who try impeachment also judge criminal prosecutions (bias, double influence); juries may be influenced by judges. Recommends a large, distinct, and publicly credible body (the Senate) with the chief justice presiding only to gain some advantages without creating double‑role problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating a separate permanent court of impeachment (costs and inconveniences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composing a court for impeachments wholly distinct from other departments would increase complexity, expense, and practical inconveniences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considers and rejects forming a permanent, separate impeachment court (either permanently salaried officers or ad hoc state officers called in) as impractical or wasteful. Implication: use existing branch (Senate) to balance practicality with independence.
